source.text: Παρῆσαν δέ τινες ἐν αὐτῷ τῷ καιρῷ ἀπαγγέλλοντες αὐτῷ περὶ τῶν Γαλιλαίων ὧν τὸ αἷμα Πιλᾶτος ἔμιξεν μετὰ τῶν θυσιῶν αὐτῶν.

records.literal_gloss: Were present now some at the very time, telling him about the Galileans, of whom the blood Pilate mixed with the sacrifices of them.

en.L: Now at that very time some were present who told {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices.
en.B: At that very time some people there told Jesus about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with the blood of their sacrifices.
en.R: Around that time some people told Jesus what had happened to some men from Galilee. Pilate had them killed while they were offering sacrifices to God. Their blood was mixed with the blood of the animals they were offering.

decisions.choice: whose blood Pilate mixed with their sacrifices: Pilate had them killed while they were offering their sacrifices
alternatives: Pilate mixed their blood into the offerings as an insult after their death
decisions.reason: The vivid phrase says that the men were killed at the very moment of worship, so that their blood ran together with the blood of the animals they had brought. Sacrifices were offered only at the temple in Jerusalem, so it happened there, probably at a festival.

decisions.choice: Pilate: the Roman governor of Judea
decisions.reason: Pontius Pilate governed Judea for Rome (3:1). This killing is not recorded anywhere else, though the Jewish historian Josephus tells of other times when Pilate's soldiers killed crowds.

decisions.choice: at that very time: while Jesus was still speaking the words of 12:54-59
decisions.reason: Luke ties the report to Jesus' warning about reading the times and settling accounts before judgment. Jesus' answer picks up that warning.

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Names Jesus where the Greek has a pronoun or leaves the subject unstated, so readers can follow who is acting.

decisions.choice: Pilate had them killed while they were offering sacrifices to God
alternatives: whose blood Pilate mixed with their sacrifices
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture of the blood.

source.text: καὶ ἀποκριθεὶς εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Δοκεῖτε ὅτι οἱ Γαλιλαῖοι οὗτοι ἁμαρτωλοὶ παρὰ πάντας τοὺς Γαλιλαίους ἐγένοντο, ὅτι ταῦτα πεπόνθασιν;

records.literal_gloss: And answering he said to them, Do you think that these Galileans sinners beyond all the Galileans were, because these things they have suffered?

en.L: And answering, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to them, "Do you think that these Galileans were sinners beyond all the [other] Galileans, because they have suffered these things?
en.B: He answered them, "Do you suppose that these Galileans suffered this because they were worse sinners than all the other people of Galilee?
en.R: Jesus answered, "Do you think this happened to them because they were worse sinners than everyone else from Galilee?

decisions.choice: sinners ... because they have suffered: the belief that a terrible death proves a person's special guilt
decisions.reason: Many assumed that great suffering was God's punishment for great sin (John 9:2; Job 4:7). Jesus raises the idea in order to reject it (13:3).

decisions.choice: beyond: more than, worse than
decisions.reason: With a comparison the word means "more than": were they greater sinners than all the rest?

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Names Jesus where the Greek has a pronoun or leaves the subject unstated, so readers can follow who is acting.

decisions.choice: the quotation opens here and runs on to 13:5
decisions.reason: Jesus' words in 13:2-5 are one answer.

source.text: οὐχί, λέγω ὑμῖν, ἀλλ’ ἐὰν μὴ μετανοῆτε πάντες ὁμοίως ἀπολεῖσθε.

records.literal_gloss: No, I say to you, but if not you repent, all likewise you will perish.

en.L: No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all perish likewise.
en.B: No, I tell you. But unless you repent, you will all perish as they did.
en.R: No, I tell you. But if you do not turn away from your sins and turn to God, you will all be destroyed too.

decisions.choice: repent: turn from sin to God, a change of heart that changes the way one lives
decisions.reason: The word means a change of mind, and in Luke it means turning back to God (3:3, 8; 5:32).

decisions.choice: perish: be destroyed and lost under God's judgment
decisions.reason: Everyone dies, so Jesus is not warning only of death. To perish is to come to ruin before God (13:28).

decisions.choice: likewise: just as surely, and perhaps in a death like theirs
decisions.reason: The word can mean simply "you too" or "in the same way". Either way the warning is to the hearers: their own judgment is coming unless they repent.

decisions.choice: turn away from your sins and turn to God (R); repent (L, B)
decisions.reason: Readable says what repenting is, as at 3:3 and 5:32.

source.text: ἢ ἐκεῖνοι οἱ δεκαοκτὼ ἐφ’ οὓς ἔπεσεν ὁ πύργος ἐν τῷ Σιλωὰμ καὶ ἀπέκτεινεν αὐτούς, δοκεῖτε ὅτι αὐτοὶ ὀφειλέται ἐγένοντο παρὰ πάντας τοὺς ἀνθρώπους τοὺς κατοικοῦντας Ἰερουσαλήμ;

records.literal_gloss: Or those eighteen on whom fell the tower in Siloam and killed them, do you think that they debtors were beyond all the men dwelling in Jerusalem?

en.L: Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them, do you think that they were debtors beyond all the {{gender:people|men}} living in Jerusalem?
en.B: Or think of those eighteen who were killed when the tower at Siloam fell on them. Do you suppose they were more guilty than everyone else living in Jerusalem?
en.R: And what about the eighteen people who died when the tower in Siloam fell on them? Do you think they were worse than all the other people who lived in Jerusalem?

decisions.choice: the tower in Siloam: a tower near the pool of Siloam in the south of Jerusalem
alternatives: a tower in a village far from the city
decisions.reason: Siloam was the area around the pool fed by Hezekiah's tunnel (John 9:7). The collapse is not recorded elsewhere. Unlike the Galileans, these people died in an accident, not by anyone's cruelty.

decisions.choice: debtors: people guilty before God
decisions.reason: Sin is pictured as a debt owed to God, as in the Lord's Prayer (11:4).

decisions.choice: more guilty (B); worse (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the picture of debt means.

decisions.choice: think of
decisions.reason: Balanced gives the fronted phrase a verb and asks the question in a second sentence.

source.text: οὐχί, λέγω ὑμῖν, ἀλλ’ ἐὰν μὴ μετανοῆτε πάντες ὡσαύτως ἀπολεῖσθε.

records.literal_gloss: No, I say to you, but if not you repent, all likewise you will perish.

en.L: No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all perish in the same way."
en.B: No, I tell you. But unless you repent, you will all perish just as they did."
en.R: No, I tell you. But if you do not turn away from your sins and turn to God, you will all be destroyed too."

decisions.choice: the same warning as 13:3, repeated for emphasis
decisions.reason: Jesus answers both stories with the same words. Luke uses a different word for "in the same way" here, but the sense is the same.

decisions.choice: turn away from your sins and turn to God (R); repent (L, B)
decisions.reason: Readable says what repenting is, as at 3:3 and 5:32.

source.text: Ἔλεγεν δὲ ταύτην τὴν παραβολήν.

records.literal_gloss: He was telling then this the parable.

en.L: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} told this parable:
en.B: Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} told this parable:
en.R: Then Jesus told them a story to teach them:

decisions.choice: parable: a story or picture drawn from daily life that teaches about God
decisions.reason: Jesus' parables make a point by comparison (8:4-10).

decisions.choice: a story to teach them
decisions.reason: Readable says what a parable is, as at 12:16.

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Names Jesus where the Greek has a pronoun or leaves the subject unstated, so readers can follow who is acting.

source.text: Συκῆν εἶχέν τις πεφυτευμένην ἐν τῷ ἀμπελῶνι αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἦλθεν ζητῶν καρπὸν ἐν αὐτῇ καὶ οὐχ εὗρεν.

records.literal_gloss: A fig tree had a certain [man] planted in the vineyard of him, and he came seeking fruit on it and not found.

en.L: "A certain [man] had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came looking for fruit on it and did not find [any].
en.B: "A man had a fig tree growing in his vineyard. He came to look for fruit on it, but found none.
en.R: "A man had a fig tree that was planted in his vineyard. He went to look for figs on it, but he did not find any.

decisions.choice: a fig tree in a vineyard: fruit trees were often planted among the vines
alternatives: a fig tree standing on its own
decisions.reason: A vineyard was a well-tended plot. A fig tree there had good soil and care, and its owner had every reason to expect figs.

decisions.choice: looking for fruit and finding none: as God looked for fruit in his people
decisions.reason: The prophets pictured Israel as God's vineyard or fig tree, and God coming to look for fruit and finding none (Isaiah 5:1-7; Jeremiah 8:13; Micah 7:1).

decisions.choice: fruit: the way of life that shows true repentance
decisions.reason: John the Baptist used the same picture: trees without good fruit are cut down (3:8-9). The parable follows the call to repent (13:3, 5).

decisions.choice: figs
decisions.reason: Readable names the fruit of a fig tree. The picture is the same.

decisions.choice: the parable is one quotation from here to 13:9, with the speakers in it in single quotation marks
alternatives: no quotation marks around the parable
decisions.reason: Jesus is speaking, and the owner and the gardener speak inside his story.

source.text: εἶπεν δὲ πρὸς τὸν ἀμπελουργόν· Ἰδοὺ τρία ἔτη ἀφ’ οὗ ἔρχομαι ζητῶν καρπὸν ἐν τῇ συκῇ ταύτῃ καὶ οὐχ εὑρίσκω· ἔκκοψον αὐτήν· ἱνατί καὶ τὴν γῆν καταργεῖ;

records.literal_gloss: He said then to the vinedresser, Look, three years from which I come seeking fruit on the fig tree this and not I find; cut down it; why even the ground does it use up?

en.L: And he said to the vinedresser, 'Look, [for] three years I have been coming looking for fruit on this fig tree, and I do not find [any]. Cut it down. Why should it even use up the ground?'
en.B: So he said to the man who tended the vineyard, 'Three years now I have come to this fig tree looking for fruit, and I never find any. Cut it down! Why should it keep wasting good ground?'
en.R: So he said to the gardener, 'For three years I have come to look for figs on this tree, and I have never found any. Cut it down! Why should it take up good ground?'

decisions.choice: three years: long enough to show that the tree will not bear
decisions.reason: A healthy fig tree bears within a few years. Three years of coming and finding nothing shows the owner's patience and that it is running out. The years are counted from when he began looking, so the tree may be older still.

decisions.choice: use up the ground: make the soil useless, taking space and goodness that another plant could use
decisions.reason: The verb means to make idle or useless. The tree is worse than fruitless: it keeps the ground from being used well.

decisions.choice: look (L); not rendered as a separate word, or "now" (B, R)
decisions.reason: Luke uses this word to draw attention to what follows. "Behold" is old-fashioned; Literal says "look", and Balanced and Readable carry the force in the flow of the sentence.

decisions.choice: the man who tended the vineyard (B); the gardener (R)
decisions.reason: "Vinedresser" is no longer an everyday word.

source.text: ὁ δὲ ἀποκριθεὶς λέγει αὐτῷ· Κύριε, ἄφες αὐτὴν καὶ τοῦτο τὸ ἔτος, ἕως ὅτου σκάψω περὶ αὐτὴν καὶ βάλω κόπρια·

records.literal_gloss: And answering he says to him, Sir, leave it also this the year, until when I dig around it and put manure;

en.L: And answering, he says to him, 'Sir, leave it this year also, until I dig around it and put [in] manure;
en.B: The man answered, 'Sir, let it stand this year too, while I dig around it and work manure into the soil.
en.R: But the gardener answered, 'Sir, let it stay one more year. I will dig around it and put fertilizer on it.

decisions.choice: Sir: a worker's respectful address to the owner
decisions.reason: The word is the one used for the Lord, but here a gardener speaks to the man who owns the vineyard.

decisions.choice: leave it: let it alone, spare it
decisions.reason: The verb can mean "forgive" (11:4), but here it means to leave the tree standing. It asks for one more year of patience.

decisions.choice: dig around it and put manure: extra care beyond what a fig tree usually needed
decisions.reason: Fig trees were not usually given such care. The gardener offers to do all that can be done before giving up.

decisions.choice: says: a present tense in a story about the past
decisions.reason: The present tense makes the scene vivid; it is told in the past at Balanced and Readable.

decisions.choice: fertilizer
decisions.reason: Readable uses the more familiar word for what manure does.

source.text: κἂν μὲν ποιήσῃ καρπὸν εἰς τὸ μέλλον εἰ δὲ μήγε, ἐκκόψεις αὐτήν.

records.literal_gloss: and if indeed it makes fruit in the coming [time] — ; but if not, you will cut it down.

en.L: and if it bears fruit in the future, [well and good]; but if not, you will cut it down.'"
en.B: If after that it bears fruit next year, well and good. If it does not, you can have it cut down.'"
en.R: Maybe it will have figs next year. If it does not, then you can cut it down.'"

decisions.choice: if it bears fruit ... : the sentence breaks off, leaving "well and good" unsaid
decisions.reason: The Greek leaves the first half unfinished, as people do in speech when the end is obvious.

decisions.choice: in the coming [time]: next year, the year that has been asked for
alternatives: at any time in the future
decisions.reason: The gardener has asked for "this year also" (13:8).

decisions.choice: you will cut it down: the owner will decide; the gardener does not refuse
decisions.reason: The gardener asks only for time. If the tree stays barren he leaves the final word to the owner.

decisions.choice: the parable ends without saying what happened: the time for repentance is real but limited
alternatives: the tree was spared for ever
decisions.reason: Jesus leaves the story open, like the warnings of 13:3 and 5. The hearers are the tree, given time to bear fruit.

decisions.choice: [well and good] (L); well and good (B); Maybe it will ... (R)
decisions.reason: The words left unsaid are supplied so the sentence can be followed; Literal puts them in brackets.

decisions.choice: you can cut it down
decisions.reason: The future here gives permission. Balanced and Readable say so.

source.text: Ἦν δὲ διδάσκων ἐν μιᾷ τῶν συναγωγῶν ἐν τοῖς σάββασιν.

records.literal_gloss: He was now teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbaths.

en.L: Now {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath.
en.B: Once, on a Sabbath, Jesus was teaching in one of the local synagogues.
en.R: One Sabbath day Jesus was teaching in a synagogue.

decisions.choice: on the Sabbaths: on a Sabbath day
decisions.reason: The plural is the usual way to name the Sabbath day (4:16).

decisions.choice: synagogues: local meeting places for prayer and the reading and teaching of Scripture
decisions.reason: This is the last time Luke shows Jesus teaching in a synagogue (4:15-16, 44; 6:6).

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Names Jesus where the Greek has a pronoun or leaves the subject unstated, so readers can follow who is acting.

source.text: καὶ ἰδοὺ γυνὴ πνεῦμα ἔχουσα ἀσθενείας ἔτη δεκαοκτώ, καὶ ἦν συγκύπτουσα καὶ μὴ δυναμένη ἀνακύψαι εἰς τὸ παντελές.

records.literal_gloss: And look, a woman a spirit having of weakness years eighteen, and was bent over and not able to straighten up completely.

en.L: And look, [there was] a woman who had had a spirit of weakness for eighteen years, and she was bent over and was not able to straighten up at all.
en.B: A woman was there whom a spirit had kept sick for eighteen years. Her back was bent, and she could not stand fully upright.
en.R: A woman was there who had been sick for eighteen years because of a spirit that made her ill. Her back was bent over, and she could not stand up straight at all.

decisions.choice: a spirit of weakness: a spirit that caused her illness
alternatives: a weak or discouraged spirit in herself
decisions.reason: Jesus says that Satan had bound her (13:16). Luke tells of an evil power behind the sickness, though he does not call it a demon or show it being driven out.

decisions.choice: completely: goes with "not able": she could not straighten up at all
alternatives: she could not straighten up fully, only part of the way
decisions.reason: The phrase can go with the verb ("straighten up completely") or with the negative ("not ... at all"). Either way she lived bent over.

decisions.choice: eighteen years: a long time of suffering, the number Jesus repeats in 13:16
decisions.reason: The same number is given for the tower at Siloam (13:4), but there is no link between the two.

decisions.choice: look (L); not rendered as a separate word, or "now" (B, R)
decisions.reason: Luke uses this word to draw attention to what follows. "Behold" is old-fashioned; Literal says "look", and Balanced and Readable carry the force in the flow of the sentence.

decisions.choice: the spirit made her sick (B); sick because of a spirit that made her ill (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "spirit of weakness" means.

source.text: ἰδὼν δὲ αὐτὴν ὁ Ἰησοῦς προσεφώνησεν καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῇ· Γύναι, ἀπολέλυσαι τῆς ἀσθενείας σου, καὶ ἐπέθηκεν αὐτῇ τὰς χεῖρας· καὶ παραχρῆμα ἀνωρθώθη, καὶ ἐδόξαζεν τὸν θεόν.

records.literal_gloss: Having seen then her Jesus called and said to her, Woman, you have been freed from the weakness of you, \v 13 and he laid on her the hands; and immediately she was made straight, and was glorifying God.

en.L: And seeing her, Jesus called [her] and said to her, "Woman, you have been set free from your weakness." \v 13 And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} laid [{{deity_pronoun:his|His}}] hands on her, and at once she was made straight, and she began glorifying God.
en.B: When Jesus saw her, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} called her over and told her, "Woman, you have been released from your illness." \v 13 Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} placed {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hands on her, and right away she stood up straight and began to give glory to God.
en.R: Jesus saw her and called her over to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. He said, "Woman, you are free from your sickness." \v 13 He put {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hands on her, and right away she was able to stand up straight. She began to give glory to God.

decisions.choice: you have been set free: the release is already done, and God is the one who has done it
decisions.reason: The perfect tense speaks of a finished act, said even before Jesus touches her. The passive points to God. The same root word is used for untying an animal and for freeing her in 13:15-16.

decisions.choice: Woman: a polite form of address
alternatives: a cold or harsh way of speaking
decisions.reason: It was a normal and respectful way to speak to a woman (John 2:4; 4:21).

decisions.choice: she was glorifying: she began to praise God, and kept on
decisions.reason: The tense pictures praise that started at once and went on.

decisions.choice: began to give glory to God
decisions.reason: Glorify is a key term; Balanced and Readable keep "glory" in an everyday phrase.

decisions.choice: [his] hands
decisions.reason: The Greek says "the hands"; Literal supplies the owner in brackets.

source.text: ἀποκριθεὶς δὲ ὁ ἀρχισυνάγωγος, ἀγανακτῶν ὅτι τῷ σαββάτῳ ἐθεράπευσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς, ἔλεγεν τῷ ὄχλῳ ὅτι Ἓξ ἡμέραι εἰσὶν ἐν αἷς δεῖ ἐργάζεσθαι· ἐν αὐταῖς οὖν ἐρχόμενοι θεραπεύεσθε καὶ μὴ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τοῦ σαββάτου.

records.literal_gloss: Answering then the synagogue ruler, being indignant that on the Sabbath had healed Jesus, was saying to the crowd that, Six days there are in which it is necessary to work; in them therefore coming be healed, and not on the day of the Sabbath.

en.L: But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, answered and was saying to the crowd, "There are six days in which [people] must work; so come on them and be healed, and not on the day of the Sabbath."
en.B: But the ruler of the synagogue was annoyed that Jesus had healed someone on the Sabbath, and he spoke up and told the crowd, "Work may be done on six days. Come to be healed on any of them, but not on the Sabbath day."
en.R: The leader of the synagogue was angry because Jesus had healed someone on the Sabbath day. He said to the people, "God's law gives us six days to work. Come and get healed on one of those days. Do not come on the Sabbath!"

decisions.choice: six days ... to work: the words of the Sabbath commandment
decisions.reason: The law says that work is to be done in six days and the seventh is a Sabbath for the Lord (Exodus 20:9-10; Deuteronomy 5:13-14). The ruler treats healing as work.

decisions.choice: healing as work: treating an illness that was not life-threatening could wait until the Sabbath was over
alternatives: all healing was banned in every case
decisions.reason: Jewish teaching allowed the Sabbath to be set aside to save a life. A woman sick for eighteen years, the ruler implies, could wait one more day.

decisions.choice: was saying to the crowd: the ruler rebukes Jesus by speaking to the people
decisions.reason: He does not address Jesus directly. Jesus' answer is addressed to him (13:15).

decisions.choice: ruler of the synagogue: the leader in charge of the synagogue's meetings
decisions.reason: As at 8:41, he arranged the services and chose who would read and teach.

decisions.choice: leader of the synagogue
decisions.reason: Readable uses a more familiar word, as at 8:41.

decisions.choice: God's law gives us
alternatives: there are six days in which one must work
decisions.reason: Readable says where the rule comes from (Exodus 20:9).

source.text: ἀπεκρίθη δὲ αὐτῷ ὁ κύριος καὶ εἶπεν· Ὑποκριταί, ἕκαστος ὑμῶν τῷ σαββάτῳ οὐ λύει τὸν βοῦν αὐτοῦ ἢ τὸν ὄνον ἀπὸ τῆς φάτνης καὶ ἀπαγαγὼν ποτίζει;

records.literal_gloss: Answered then him the Lord and said, Hypocrites, each of you on the Sabbath not unties the ox of him or the donkey from the manger and having led [it] away gives drink?

en.L: But the Lord answered him and said, "Hypocrites! Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie {{gender:their|his}} ox or donkey from the manger and lead [it] away to give [it] drink?
en.B: The Lord answered him, "You hypocrites! On the Sabbath every one of you unties your ox or your donkey from its stall and takes it out for water, do you not?
en.R: The Lord Jesus answered him, "You are pretending! On the Sabbath day every one of you unties your ox or your donkey. You lead it out of its stall so it can drink water.

decisions.choice: the Lord: Luke the narrator calls Jesus by his title
decisions.reason: As at 7:13 and 12:42, Luke uses the title for Jesus as he tells the story.

decisions.choice: hypocrites: people playing a part, whose words do not match their own practice
decisions.reason: The ruler and those who agree with him (13:17) apply the Sabbath strictly to this woman but not to their own animals (12:1, 56).

decisions.choice: untying an animal and leading it to water on the Sabbath: something everyone did
decisions.reason: Jesus' question assumes that his hearers all did this. An animal could not go without water for a day.

decisions.choice: manger: the feeding place, the stall where the animal was tied
decisions.reason: It is the same word as in 2:7, where it means a feeding trough.

decisions.choice: the Lord Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable names Jesus, as at 7:13.

decisions.choice: You are pretending!
decisions.reason: Readable says what hypocrisy is, as at 12:56.

decisions.choice: a statement (R), or a statement with a question added (B)
decisions.reason: The question expects the answer "yes". Balanced and Readable state it.

source.text: ταύτην δὲ θυγατέρα Ἀβραὰμ οὖσαν, ἣν ἔδησεν ὁ Σατανᾶς ἰδοὺ δέκα καὶ ὀκτὼ ἔτη, οὐκ ἔδει λυθῆναι ἀπὸ τοῦ δεσμοῦ τούτου τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τοῦ σαββάτου;

records.literal_gloss: This now a daughter of Abraham being, whom bound Satan, look, ten and eight years, not was it necessary to be loosed from the bond this on the day of the Sabbath?

en.L: And this [woman], being a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound, look, ten and eight years, was it not necessary that she be loosed from this bond on the day of the Sabbath?"
en.B: And here is a daughter of Abraham whom Satan has kept tied up for eighteen whole years. Should she not be untied from this bond on the Sabbath day?"
en.R: This woman is a daughter of Abraham, one of God's own people. Satan has kept her tied up for eighteen years! Surely it was right to untie her on the Sabbath day!"

decisions.choice: a daughter of Abraham: a Jewish woman, one of the people of God's promise
alternatives: a descendant of Abraham only by birth
decisions.reason: Abraham's children are the people God made his promises to (1:55, 73). Jesus uses the same kind of name for Zacchaeus (19:9). She belongs to God's people and deserves better than an animal.

decisions.choice: Satan has bound her: her illness is the work of Satan, and healing her frees her from his power
alternatives: a way of saying that she was ill
decisions.reason: Luke speaks of Jesus healing all who were oppressed by the devil (Acts 10:38), and of Jesus overpowering the strong man (11:21-22).

decisions.choice: was it not necessary: the same word the ruler used ("there are six days in which one must work", 13:14)
decisions.reason: Jesus turns the ruler's word around. It was not merely allowed to free her on the Sabbath; it was what had to be done. The day of rest is the right day for release.

decisions.choice: loosed from this bond: the same verb as "untie" the ox in 13:15
decisions.reason: Jesus argues from the smaller to the greater. If an animal is untied on the Sabbath, how much more should this woman be.

decisions.choice: look (L); not rendered as a separate word, or "now" (B, R)
decisions.reason: Luke uses this word to draw attention to what follows. "Behold" is old-fashioned; Literal says "look", and Balanced and Readable carry the force in the flow of the sentence.

decisions.choice: one of God's own people
decisions.reason: Readable explains what being Abraham's daughter means.

decisions.choice: ten and eight years (L); eighteen whole years (B)
decisions.reason: The Greek spells out "ten and eight" for emphasis, and adds "look". Literal keeps the form; Balanced conveys the emphasis with "whole".

source.text: καὶ ταῦτα λέγοντος αὐτοῦ κατῃσχύνοντο πάντες οἱ ἀντικείμενοι αὐτῷ, καὶ πᾶς ὁ ὄχλος ἔχαιρεν ἐπὶ πᾶσιν τοῖς ἐνδόξοις τοῖς γινομένοις ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: And these things saying of him were put to shame all those opposing him, and all the crowd was rejoicing over all the glorious things being done by him.

en.L: And as {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said these things, all those opposing {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} were put to shame, and all the crowd was rejoicing over all the glorious things being done by {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.
en.B: When {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said this, everyone who had set themselves against {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} was put to shame, while the whole crowd rejoiced at all the glorious things {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was doing.
en.R: When Jesus said these things, all the people who were against {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} felt ashamed. But the crowd was very happy. They saw all the amazing things {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was doing.

decisions.choice: were put to shame: were shown up in public as wrong
decisions.reason: In front of the whole synagogue they had no answer.

decisions.choice: all those opposing him were put to shame: wording found in Isaiah 45:16 in the ancient Greek translation
decisions.reason: Isaiah says that those who oppose God will be put to shame. Luke's words are very close to that passage in Greek.

decisions.choice: the glorious things: wonderful deeds that showed God's power
decisions.reason: The healings were signs of God at work (7:16).

decisions.choice: amazing things
decisions.reason: Readable uses the everyday word. This word is related to glory but is not the key term.

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Names Jesus where the Greek has a pronoun or leaves the subject unstated, so readers can follow who is acting.

source.text: Ἔλεγεν οὖν· Τίνι ὁμοία ἐστὶν ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ τίνι ὁμοιώσω αὐτήν;

records.literal_gloss: He was saying therefore, To what like is the kingdom of God, and to what shall I liken it?

en.L: So {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was saying, "What is the kingdom of God like, and to what shall I liken it?
en.B: So {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, "What is the kingdom of God like? What picture shall I use for it?
en.R: Then Jesus said, "What is the kingdom of God like? What can I use to show you what it is like?

decisions.choice: therefore: the parables follow from what has just happened
alternatives: a new start with no link
decisions.reason: The word ties the sayings to the healing. A woman freed in one synagogue looks small, but the kingdom grows from such beginnings.

decisions.choice: two questions: a teacher's way of introducing a comparison
decisions.reason: Jesus asks the questions in order to answer them himself (Isaiah 40:18).

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Names Jesus where the Greek has a pronoun or leaves the subject unstated, so readers can follow who is acting.

decisions.choice: the quotation opens here and closes at the end of 13:19
decisions.reason: Luke says "and again he said" at 13:20, so each parable has its own quotation.

source.text: ὁμοία ἐστὶν κόκκῳ σινάπεως, ὃν λαβὼν ἄνθρωπος ἔβαλεν εἰς κῆπον ἑαυτοῦ, καὶ ηὔξησεν καὶ ἐγένετο εἰς δένδρον, καὶ τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ κατεσκήνωσεν ἐν τοῖς κλάδοις αὐτοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: Like it is to a grain of mustard, which having taken a man threw into garden of himself, and it grew and became into a tree, and the birds of the sky nested in the branches of it.

en.L: It is like a grain of mustard, which a man took and threw into his own garden; and it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the sky nested in its branches."
en.B: It is like this: a man took a mustard seed and sowed it in his own garden. It kept growing until it was a tree, and birds of the air came and nested among its branches."
en.R: It is like a tiny mustard seed. A man planted it in his garden. It grew and grew until it became a tree. Then birds came and built nests in its branches."

decisions.choice: a grain of mustard: a tiny seed that grows into a plant as tall as a person or taller
decisions.reason: The mustard seed was known for being very small (17:6). The plant that grew from it could reach several feet high in a garden.

decisions.choice: the birds nesting in its branches: a picture of a great kingdom sheltering many nations
decisions.reason: The prophets used the picture of a great tree with birds in its branches for a kingdom (Daniel 4; Ezekiel 17:23; 31:6). The kingdom of God begins small and becomes great.

decisions.choice: threw: sowed, planted
decisions.reason: The verb is used for scattering or sowing seed.

decisions.choice: tiny
decisions.reason: Readable says why a mustard seed was chosen: it is very small.

decisions.choice: mustard seed
decisions.reason: "Grain" here means a single seed.

source.text: Καὶ πάλιν εἶπεν· Τίνι ὁμοιώσω τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ;

records.literal_gloss: And again he said, To what shall I liken the kingdom of God?

en.L: And again {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, "To what shall I liken the kingdom of God?
en.B: Once more {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, "With what shall I compare the kingdom of God?
en.R: Then Jesus said again, "What can I compare the kingdom of God to?

decisions.choice: again: a second picture with the same point, as Jesus often pairs a man and a woman
decisions.reason: The mustard seed and the yeast belong together, like the shepherd and the woman in 15:3-10.

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Names Jesus where the Greek has a pronoun or leaves the subject unstated, so readers can follow who is acting.

source.text: ὁμοία ἐστὶν ζύμῃ, ἣν λαβοῦσα γυνὴ ἔκρυψεν εἰς ἀλεύρου σάτα τρία ἕως οὗ ἐζυμώθη ὅλον.

records.literal_gloss: Like it is to leaven, which having taken a woman hid into of flour measures three, until was leavened all.

en.L: It is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour until all [of it] was leavened."
en.B: It is like yeast. A woman took some and hid it in {{units:about 40 pounds|three measures}} of flour, and in time the whole batch rose."
en.R: It is like yeast. A woman mixed a little yeast into a big batch of flour, {{units:about 40 pounds|three measures}}. The yeast worked its way through until all the dough had risen."

decisions.choice: leaven: a lump of old, fermented dough kept back to make the next batch rise
decisions.reason: A little leaven works through a whole batch of dough (12:1). Here the picture is of something small and hidden that spreads through everything, for good.

decisions.choice: hid: mixed in, so that it could not be seen
alternatives: put away to keep it safe
decisions.reason: The word is unusual for mixing dough, and it fits the point: the kingdom is at work even when it is hidden.

decisions.choice: three measures of flour: a very large amount, enough bread for a great many people
decisions.reason: A measure (saton) was a dry measure of perhaps 7 to 13 liters; the estimates vary. Sarah baked from three measures of flour for her three visitors (Genesis 18:6).

decisions.choice: yeast (B, R); leaven (L)
decisions.reason: "Leaven" is no longer an everyday word, as at 12:1.

decisions.choice: about 40 pounds by default; "three measures" as the Measures alternative
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the unit, called a measure as at John 2:6. The size of a saton is uncertain, so the figure is approximate.

decisions.choice: a little yeast
decisions.reason: Readable says what the parable assumes: a little yeast affects a lot of dough.

source.text: Καὶ διεπορεύετο κατὰ πόλεις καὶ κώμας διδάσκων καὶ πορείαν ποιούμενος εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα.

records.literal_gloss: And he was going through by towns and villages, teaching and journey making toward Jerusalem.

en.L: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was going through towns and villages one after another, teaching and making a journey toward Jerusalem.
en.B: Jesus traveled on from town to town and village to village, teaching, and pressing on toward Jerusalem.
en.R: Jesus kept going through the towns and villages. He taught the people there as {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} traveled on toward Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: toward Jerusalem: Luke reminds his readers of the journey Jesus set out on in 9:51
alternatives: a short trip to the city
decisions.reason: Jesus is going to Jerusalem to die and rise (9:22, 51; 13:33).

decisions.choice: through towns and villages: from one place to the next
decisions.reason: The phrase pictures him moving from place to place.

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Names Jesus where the Greek has a pronoun or leaves the subject unstated, so readers can follow who is acting.

source.text: εἶπεν δέ τις αὐτῷ· Κύριε, εἰ ὀλίγοι οἱ σῳζόμενοι;

records.literal_gloss: Said then someone to him, Lord, [are] few those being saved?

en.L: And someone said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Lord, are those being saved few?"
en.B: Someone asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Lord, is it only a few who are being saved?"
en.R: Someone said to Jesus, "Lord, will God save only a small number of people?"

decisions.choice: if: here it introduces a direct question
decisions.reason: Luke sometimes uses this word to open a direct question (22:49).

decisions.choice: those being saved: those whom God is rescuing from judgment and bringing into his kingdom
decisions.reason: The present tense speaks of people on the way to that rescue (Acts 2:47). Jesus' answer is about entering the kingdom (13:24-29).

decisions.choice: will God save
decisions.reason: Readable names God as the one who saves, which the passive implies.

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Names Jesus where the Greek has a pronoun or leaves the subject unstated, so readers can follow who is acting.

source.text: ὁ δὲ εἶπεν πρὸς αὐτούς·

records.literal_gloss: And he said to them,

en.L: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to them,
en.B: He said to them,
en.R: Jesus said to all of them,

decisions.choice: to them: Jesus answers everyone present, not just the one who asked
decisions.reason: The question was about others; Jesus turns it into a call to his hearers themselves.

decisions.choice: all of them
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that the answer goes to everyone.

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Names Jesus where the Greek has a pronoun or leaves the subject unstated, so readers can follow who is acting.

source.text: Ἀγωνίζεσθε εἰσελθεῖν διὰ τῆς στενῆς θύρας, ὅτι πολλοί, λέγω ὑμῖν, ζητήσουσιν εἰσελθεῖν καὶ οὐκ ἰσχύσουσιν, ἀφ’ οὗ ἂν ἐγερθῇ ὁ οἰκοδεσπότης καὶ ἀποκλείσῃ τὴν θύραν, καὶ ἄρξησθε ἔξω ἑστάναι καὶ κρούειν τὴν θύραν λέγοντες· Κύριε, ἄνοιξον ἡμῖν· καὶ ἀποκριθεὶς ἐρεῖ ὑμῖν· Οὐκ οἶδα ὑμᾶς πόθεν ἐστέ.

records.literal_gloss: Strive to enter through the narrow door, because many, I say to you, will seek to enter and not will be able, \v 25 from when has risen the master of the house and has shut the door, and you begin outside to stand and to knock the door saying, Lord, open to us, and answering he will say to you, Not I know you from where you are.

en.L: "Strive to enter through the narrow door, because many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able, \v 25 once the master of the house has risen and shut the door, and you begin to stand outside and to knock on the door, saying, 'Lord, open to us,' and he will answer and say to you, 'I do not know you, where you are from.'
en.B: "Struggle hard to get in through the narrow door. Many people, I tell you, will look for a way in and will fail. \v 25 When the master of the house has risen and locked the door, you will find yourselves outside. You will knock and call out, 'Lord, open up for us!' And his answer to you will be, 'I do not know you; I do not know where you are from.'
en.R: "Work hard to go in through the narrow door. I tell you, many people will try to go in, but they will not be able to. \v 25 The master of the house will get up and shut the door. Then you will stand outside and knock on the door. You will say, 'Lord, open the door for us!' But he will say, 'I do not know you. I do not know where you come from.'

decisions.choice: strive: struggle with all one's strength, as in a contest
decisions.reason: The word was used for athletes competing for a prize. Jesus does not answer how many will be saved; he tells his hearers to make sure they enter.

decisions.choice: the narrow door: the way into the kingdom, open now but not for ever
decisions.reason: The door is narrow and will be shut. The time to enter is now, by turning to God while Jesus calls (13:3, 5).

decisions.choice: 13:25 continues the sentence of 13:24: many will not be able to enter once the door is shut
alternatives: 13:25 begins a new sentence, completed in 13:26: "when the master has shut the door ... then you will begin to say"
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT joins the verses with a comma. Some editions start a new sentence at 13:25. The meaning is much the same: the door closes and latecomers are kept out.

decisions.choice: I do not know where you are from: you are strangers to me, not part of my household
alternatives: I do not know your hometown
decisions.reason: The master disowns them. He does not recognize them as his own (Matthew 25:12).

decisions.choice: the master of the house: a figure in the picture who stands for Jesus
decisions.reason: Those outside say that they ate with him and that he taught in their streets (13:26), which describes Jesus' own ministry.

decisions.choice: Lord
decisions.reason: The people at the door address the master of the house with the title that also means the Lord, as people call Jesus "Lord" in 6:46.

decisions.choice: several short sentences
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable break the long sentence so it can be followed aloud.

decisions.choice: the quotation opens here and runs on to 13:30; the words of the people and the master are in single quotation marks
decisions.reason: Jesus' answer in 13:24-30 is one speech.

source.text: τότε ἄρξεσθε λέγειν· Ἐφάγομεν ἐνώπιόν σου καὶ ἐπίομεν, καὶ ἐν ταῖς πλατείαις ἡμῶν ἐδίδαξας·

records.literal_gloss: Then you will begin to say, We ate in presence of you and drank, and in the streets of us you taught;

en.L: Then you will begin to say, 'We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets.'
en.B: Then you will begin to protest, 'We ate and drank in your company, and it was in our streets that you taught!'
en.R: Then you will say, 'We ate and drank with you! You taught in the streets of our town!'

decisions.choice: we ate and drank in your presence: we shared meals with you
alternatives: we ate at a feast you gave
decisions.reason: Eating together was a sign of friendship. They claim to know him because they were near him.

decisions.choice: you taught in our streets: they heard Jesus but did not respond
decisions.reason: Being near Jesus and hearing him is not the same as entering through the door. The picture of the master of the house here shows Jesus himself.

decisions.choice: you, with no capital option
decisions.reason: The people are speaking to the master of the house in the picture. Although he stands for Jesus, pronouns for a figure in a parable are not treated as pronouns for God or Christ.

source.text: καὶ ἐρεῖ λέγων ὑμῖν· Οὐκ οἶδα πόθεν ἐστέ· ἀπόστητε ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ, πάντες ἐργάται ἀδικίας.

records.literal_gloss: And he will say, telling you, Not I know from where you are; depart from me, all workers of unrighteousness.

en.L: And he will say, telling you, 'I do not know where you are from. Depart from me, all [you] workers of unrighteousness.'
en.B: But he will tell you, 'I do not know where you come from. Go away from me, all of you whose work is wrongdoing!'
en.R: But he will say to you again, 'I do not know where you come from. Go away from me, all of you who do evil things!'

decisions.choice: and he will say, telling you: the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: and he will say, "I tell you, I do not know ...", the reading of many manuscripts
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts have "I tell you" as part of the master's words, and some leave out the words "I tell you" or "telling you" altogether. The sense is the same: the master repeats his answer. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: depart from me, all workers of unrighteousness: words from Psalm 6:9
alternatives: Jesus' own words with no source
decisions.reason: In the psalm the one praying tells all evildoers to leave him, because the Lord has heard him. Here the master says them to those he sends away.

decisions.choice: unrighteousness: wrongdoing, injustice
decisions.reason: The word is the opposite of what is right and just.

decisions.choice: again
decisions.reason: The master repeats what he said in 13:25. Readable makes the repeat clear.

decisions.choice: all of you whose work is wrongdoing (B); all of you who do evil things (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the picture of work in plain words; Readable says it simply.

source.text: ἐκεῖ ἔσται ὁ κλαυθμὸς καὶ ὁ βρυγμὸς τῶν ὀδόντων, ὅταν ὄψησθε Ἀβραὰμ καὶ Ἰσαὰκ καὶ Ἰακὼβ καὶ πάντας τοὺς προφήτας ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τοῦ θεοῦ, ὑμᾶς δὲ ἐκβαλλομένους ἔξω.

records.literal_gloss: There will be the weeping and the grinding of the teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, but you being thrown out outside.

en.L: There will be weeping and grinding of teeth there, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, but yourselves being thrown outside.
en.B: You will weep there and grind your teeth when you see Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and every one of the prophets inside the kingdom of God, and yourselves driven out.
en.R: You will cry and grind your teeth in anger and pain. You will see Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the prophets in the kingdom of God. But you will be thrown outside.

decisions.choice: weeping and grinding of teeth: bitter grief and anguish
decisions.reason: Weeping shows grief; grinding the teeth shows anguish and anger (Psalm 112:10). Together they picture the despair of those shut out.

decisions.choice: there: outside the shut door
decisions.reason: The word points back to the place outside the house (13:25).

decisions.choice: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the prophets in the kingdom: the fathers of Israel at God's feast
decisions.reason: The hearers expected to share the kingdom with the ancestors of their people. Instead they see them inside while they are outside (13:29; 16:22-23).

decisions.choice: You will weep there ...
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make the hearers the subject, which the context makes clear.

decisions.choice: in anger and pain
decisions.reason: Readable explains what grinding the teeth shows.

source.text: καὶ ἥξουσιν ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν καὶ δυσμῶν καὶ ἀπὸ βορρᾶ καὶ νότου καὶ ἀνακλιθήσονται ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τοῦ θεοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: And they will come from east and west and from north and south and will recline in the kingdom of God.

en.L: And they will come from east and west and from north and south, and will recline [at table] in the kingdom of God.
en.B: And others will arrive from east and west, from north and south, and sit down to eat in the kingdom of God.
en.R: People will come from all over the world, from the east, west, north, and south. They will sit down and eat together in the kingdom of God.

decisions.choice: from east and west and from north and south: God gathering his people from every direction
alternatives: from the regions around Israel only
decisions.reason: The prophets and psalms speak of God gathering people from the four directions (Psalm 107:3; Isaiah 43:5-6), and of a feast for all peoples (Isaiah 25:6).

decisions.choice: recline: lie on couches at a feast
decisions.reason: At a formal meal guests reclined at the table. The kingdom is pictured as a great banquet (14:15).

decisions.choice: they: people from all over the world, including those from other nations
decisions.reason: The subject is not named. In contrast with "you" who are thrown out, they come from far away. Luke tells later of the good news going to all nations (24:47).

decisions.choice: others (B); People (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the verb a subject, to make the contrast with "you" clear.

decisions.choice: from all over the world
decisions.reason: Readable says what the four directions mean.

source.text: καὶ ἰδοὺ εἰσὶν ἔσχατοι οἳ ἔσονται πρῶτοι, καὶ εἰσὶν πρῶτοι οἳ ἔσονται ἔσχατοι.

records.literal_gloss: And look, there are last who will be first, and there are first who will be last.

en.L: And look, there are last who will be first, and there are first who will be last."
en.B: Some who are last now will be first, and some who are first now will be last."
en.R: Some people who are treated as least important now will be most important then. And some who are most important now will be least important then."

decisions.choice: last ... first: God will reverse the places people hold now
decisions.reason: Luke often shows God bringing down the proud and lifting up the humble (1:52-53; 14:11; 18:14). Those who expected to be first may be shut out.

decisions.choice: there are last who ...: some, not all
decisions.reason: The saying speaks of some people, not of every case.

decisions.choice: look (L); not rendered as a separate word, or "now" (B, R)
decisions.reason: Luke uses this word to draw attention to what follows. "Behold" is old-fashioned; Literal says "look", and Balanced and Readable carry the force in the flow of the sentence.

decisions.choice: now ... then
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make clear that the reversal is between this life and the kingdom.

source.text: Ἐν αὐτῇ τῇ ὥρᾳ προσῆλθάν τινες Φαρισαῖοι λέγοντες αὐτῷ· Ἔξελθε καὶ πορεύου ἐντεῦθεν, ὅτι Ἡρῴδης θέλει σε ἀποκτεῖναι.

records.literal_gloss: In same the hour came some Pharisees saying to him, Go out and go from here, because Herod wants you to kill.

en.L: At that very hour some Pharisees came, saying to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Get out and go from here, because Herod wants to kill {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}."
en.B: At that very time some Pharisees came up to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} with a warning: "Get away from here and be on {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} way, because Herod intends to kill {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}."
en.R: Right then some Pharisees came to Jesus. They told {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Get out of this area! Herod wants to kill {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}."

decisions.choice: Pharisees: a Jewish movement devoted to keeping the law of Moses in every part of daily life
decisions.reason: They were respected teachers among the people, and often questioned Jesus (5:21; 11:37-54).

decisions.choice: Herod: Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee and Perea
decisions.reason: This is the son of the Herod of 1:5. He had put John the Baptist to death and wondered who Jesus was (3:19-20; 9:7-9).

decisions.choice: the Pharisees' motive is not stated
alternatives: they were trying to help him
they wanted to frighten him away
decisions.reason: Some Pharisees may have wanted to warn Jesus; others may have wanted him out of their area. Luke does not say.

decisions.choice: with a warning
decisions.reason: Balanced names what their words were.

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Names Jesus where the Greek has a pronoun or leaves the subject unstated, so readers can follow who is acting.

source.text: καὶ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Πορευθέντες εἴπατε τῇ ἀλώπεκι ταύτῃ· Ἰδοὺ ἐκβάλλω δαιμόνια καὶ ἰάσεις ἀποτελῶ σήμερον καὶ αὔριον, καὶ τῇ τρίτῃ τελειοῦμαι.

records.literal_gloss: And he said to them, Having gone say to the fox this, Look, I cast out demons and healings I complete today and tomorrow, and on the third I am completed.

en.L: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to them, "Go and tell that fox, 'Look, I cast out demons and complete healings today and tomorrow, and on the third [day] I am brought to completion.'
en.B: He answered them, "Go and tell that fox: 'Today and tomorrow I cast out demons and carry out cures, and on the third day I finish {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} course.'
en.R: Jesus said to them, "Go and tell that fox Herod, 'Today and tomorrow I am forcing demons out of people and healing the sick. On the third day I will finish {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} work.'

decisions.choice: that fox: a sly, cunning and destructive man
decisions.reason: The fox was a picture of slyness and of destroying what others had built (Ezekiel 13:4; Song of Songs 2:15). Jesus is not afraid of Herod.

decisions.choice: today and tomorrow, and on the third day: a short time already fixed
decisions.reason: The phrase speaks of a short, set time (Hosea 6:2). Jesus will finish his work on his own timetable, not Herod's.

decisions.choice: I am brought to completion: I reach the goal of my work, which points to his death in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: The verb means to bring to completion or to the goal. Jesus goes on to speak of a prophet dying in Jerusalem (13:33), and his "completion" there includes his death and being raised (12:50; 18:31-33).

decisions.choice: healings: cures of the sick
decisions.reason: The word means acts of healing.

decisions.choice: look (L); not rendered as a separate word, or "now" (B, R)
decisions.reason: Luke uses this word to draw attention to what follows. "Behold" is old-fashioned; Literal says "look", and Balanced and Readable carry the force in the flow of the sentence.

decisions.choice: I finish my course (B); I will finish my work (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say plainly what is completed. Literal keeps the passive.

decisions.choice: Herod
decisions.reason: Readable names the person meant by "fox".

decisions.choice: the quotation opens here and runs on to 13:35; the message for Herod is in single quotation marks
decisions.reason: Jesus' words in 13:32-35 are one speech.

source.text: πλὴν δεῖ με σήμερον καὶ αὔριον καὶ τῇ ἐχομένῃ πορεύεσθαι, ὅτι οὐκ ἐνδέχεται προφήτην ἀπολέσθαι ἔξω Ἰερουσαλήμ.

records.literal_gloss: But it is necessary me today and tomorrow and the following to travel, because not it is possible a prophet to perish outside of Jerusalem.

en.L: But it is necessary for {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} to travel on today and tomorrow and the following [day], because it is not possible for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem.
en.B: But I must go on {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} way today, tomorrow, and the day after, because it cannot be that a prophet should die anywhere but in Jerusalem.
en.R: But I must keep traveling today, tomorrow, and the next day. After all, a prophet cannot be killed anywhere except in Jerusalem!

decisions.choice: it is necessary: it is God's plan for Jesus
decisions.reason: Luke uses this word for what must happen to Jesus by God's will (9:22; 17:25; 24:7, 26).

decisions.choice: it is not possible for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem: bitter irony
alternatives: a rule or law about where prophets die
decisions.reason: Prophets had died elsewhere, John the Baptist among them. Jesus speaks bitterly: Jerusalem is the city that kills the prophets (13:34; 11:47-51; Jeremiah 26:20-23).

decisions.choice: travel: go on with his journey
decisions.reason: Jesus will not hurry away from Herod; he will keep going toward Jerusalem (9:51; 13:22).

decisions.choice: After all
decisions.reason: Readable signals the irony.

source.text: Ἰερουσαλὴμ Ἰερουσαλήμ, ἡ ἀποκτείνουσα τοὺς προφήτας καὶ λιθοβολοῦσα τοὺς ἀπεσταλμένους πρὸς αὐτήν ποσάκις ἠθέλησα ἐπισυνάξαι τὰ τέκνα σου ὃν τρόπον ὄρνις τὴν ἑαυτῆς νοσσιὰν ὑπὸ τὰς πτέρυγας, καὶ οὐκ ἠθελήσατε.

records.literal_gloss: Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the one killing the prophets and stoning those sent to her, how often I wanted to gather the children of you in the way a hen the own brood under the wings, and not you were willing.

en.L: Jerusalem, Jerusalem, [you] who kill the prophets and stone those sent to her! How often I wanted to gather your children, in the way a hen [gathers] her brood under [her] wings, and you were not willing!
en.B: Jerusalem, Jerusalem! You kill the prophets and stone the messengers sent to you. How many times I wanted to gather your children, the way a hen keeps her young ones under her wings! But you refused.
en.R: Jerusalem, Jerusalem! You kill the prophets. You throw stones at the messengers God sends to you. Many times I wanted to gather your people together and protect them, the way a hen tucks her chicks under her wings. But you would not let {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

decisions.choice: your children: the people of Jerusalem
alternatives: only the children of the city
decisions.reason: A city's people were called its children (19:44).

decisions.choice: a hen gathering her brood under her wings: God's care and protection for his people
decisions.reason: The Scriptures picture God sheltering his people under his wings (Deuteronomy 32:11; Ruth 2:12; Psalm 91:4).

decisions.choice: how often I wanted: Jesus speaks of a longing for Jerusalem that goes beyond his own visits
alternatives: only the times Jesus had been in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Luke does not tell of many visits to Jerusalem. Jesus speaks the way God speaks of sending his messengers again and again (2 Chronicles 36:15-16).

decisions.choice: stoning those sent to her: putting God's messengers to death
alternatives: throwing stones to drive them away
decisions.reason: The prophet Zechariah was stoned in the temple court (2 Chronicles 24:20-21). Stoning was the law's punishment for a false prophet (Deuteronomy 13); Jerusalem used it on true ones.

decisions.choice: those sent to her
decisions.reason: The Greek speaks to the city and then of it in the same sentence. Literal keeps that change; Balanced and Readable say "you" throughout.

decisions.choice: God sends; you would not let me
alternatives: those sent; you were not willing
decisions.reason: Readable names God as the sender and says what the city refused.

decisions.choice: your people
decisions.reason: Readable explains the idiom.

source.text: ἰδοὺ ἀφίεται ὑμῖν ὁ οἶκος ὑμῶν.

records.literal_gloss: Look, is left to you the house of you.

en.L: Look, your house is left to you.
en.B: Now your house is left to you.
en.R: Now your house is left to you, for you to keep on your own.

decisions.choice: your house is left to you: the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: your house is left to you desolate, the reading of many manuscripts
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add "desolate", as in Matthew 23:38. The earliest manuscripts of Luke do not have it. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: your house: the temple, or the city and its people
decisions.reason: The house may be the temple, God's house, or Jerusalem itself as the home of its people. Either way, God is leaving it to them without his protection.

decisions.choice: left to you: abandoned by God
decisions.reason: The prophets warned that God would abandon his house (Jeremiah 12:7; 22:5). Jesus later weeps over the city's coming destruction (19:41-44).

decisions.choice: look (L); not rendered as a separate word, or "now" (B, R)
decisions.reason: Luke uses this word to draw attention to what follows. "Behold" is old-fashioned; Literal says "look", and Balanced and Readable carry the force in the flow of the sentence.

decisions.choice: for you to keep on your own
decisions.reason: Readable explains what being "left" means without adding "desolate", the later reading noted in m1.

source.text: λέγω δὲ ὑμῖν, οὐ μὴ ἴδητέ με ἕως ἥξει ὅτε εἴπητε· Εὐλογημένος ὁ ἐρχόμενος ἐν ὀνόματι κυρίου.

records.literal_gloss: I say then to you, not not you will see me until it will come when you say, Blessed the one coming in name of Lord.

en.L: And I tell you, you will not see {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} until [the time] comes when you say, 'Blessed [is] the one who comes in [the] name of [the] Lord.'"
en.B: I tell you, you will not see {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} until the time comes when you say, 'Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord.'"
en.R: I tell you, you will not see {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} until the time when you say, 'May God bless the one who comes in the Lord's name!'"

decisions.choice: Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord: Psalm 118:26
decisions.reason: The psalm was sung by pilgrims coming to the temple at the festivals. Where the Greek has "Lord", the Hebrew of the psalm has the divine name, YHWH. The crowd uses these words when Jesus rides into Jerusalem (19:38).

decisions.choice: until the time comes when you say: the day Jerusalem welcomes him
alternatives: only his entry into Jerusalem in 19:38
only his coming at the end of the age
decisions.reason: Jesus may mean his entry into the city, when his followers say these words, or his coming in glory, when the city will welcome him. Luke does not settle it.

decisions.choice: until [the time] comes when: the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: until you say, the reading of some manuscripts
decisions.reason: Manuscripts differ over the words between "until" and "you say". The sense is the same. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: not ... see me: a strong double negative, "you will certainly not see me"
decisions.reason: The Greek uses two negatives together for emphasis.

decisions.choice: May God bless
decisions.reason: This word for blessed is a prayer that God will bless, not the word of the Beatitudes. Readable makes the prayer clear.

decisions.choice: in the Lord's name
alternatives: in the name of the Lord
decisions.reason: Readable uses a shorter form.
